title: Can You Really Be Friends With an Ex?
metaTitle: Can You Really Be Friends With an Ex?
metaDescription: Sometimes yes, sometimes not. Research suggests it depends on your reasons and feelings. Here is what the data shows, presented neutrally.
keyFinding: Friendship with an ex can work and can be healthy, but whether it does appears to depend heavily on the reasons for staying in contact and whether both people have emotionally moved on, with outcomes worse when one harbours unresolved feelings or it blocks moving forward.
honestAnswer: Sometimes — it depends on the reasons and the feelings involved. Research on post-relationship friendship suggests that people stay friends with exes for very different motives, and those motives seem to predict how the friendship goes. When the basis is genuine friendship or practical shared responsibilities and both people have moved on emotionally, it can work and be healthy.

When one or both people are holding onto unresolved romantic or sexual feelings, or the friendship mainly serves to avoid the discomfort of letting go, it more often stalls healing rather than supporting it. So the honest answer is neither 'always fine' nor 'never works' — it depends largely on the why.
whatDataShows: Work by Justin Mogilski and Lisa Welling on reasons for staying friends with exes found that the motives fall into recognisable groups — including genuine friendship and reliability, practical considerations like shared finances or children, sentimentality, and lingering romantic or sexual desire. Crucially, these different reasons were associated with different outcomes rather than all being equal.

The broad pattern in this and related research is that friendship-based and practical motives tend to be associated with more positive, lower-conflict outcomes, while motives rooted in unresolved romantic or sexual hope are associated with more negative ones, including jealousy and difficulty moving on. The reason behind the contact appears to matter more than the mere fact of staying in touch.

How the relationship ended and each person's attachment style also appear to play a role. Research on post-breakup adjustment suggests that breakups that were mutual or amicable, and people who are more securely attached, tend to navigate post-relationship friendship more smoothly, while a contested ending or anxious attachment can make continued contact harder and slower to settle.
whyItFeelsDifferent: It can feel like there should be a single right answer — that staying friends is either the mature thing to do or a clear mistake — when the research suggests the same arrangement can be healthy for one pair and harmful for another. The deciding factor is less the label 'friends with an ex' and more the underlying motives and feelings, which are easy to misread, including in oneself.

It also feels different because people are not always honest with themselves about why they are staying in touch. A friendship maintained partly in the hope of rekindling things can look, from the outside and even from the inside, like a purely platonic one. That gap between the stated reason and the real one is part of why outcomes vary so widely.

And the social scripts pull in opposite directions. One says cutting contact completely is the only clean way to heal; another says a 'good breakup' means staying close. Neither is universally right in the data, which points instead to a case-by-case picture shaped by the reasons, the feelings, and how the relationship ended.
whatResearchSaysToDo: Where the research offers practical guidance, it points toward being honest about the motive. Friendships grounded in genuine liking, or in practical necessities like co-parenting or shared finances, tend to fare better, so naming your actual reason — to yourself first — is a reasonable starting point for judging whether a friendship is likely to help or hinder.

The evidence also suggests that having genuinely moved on emotionally, on both sides, is associated with better outcomes. Where strong feelings remain unresolved, the literature on post-breakup adjustment broadly supports giving those feelings time and space to settle before attempting a close friendship, since contact too soon can slow that process.

For relationships with ongoing practical ties — especially shared children — a workable, lower-intimacy form of contact focused on those responsibilities is a common and reasonable arrangement, distinct from the closer friendships the research finds more contingent on having moved on. The right form of contact depends on what it is actually for.
whatDoesNotHelp: Staying friends as a way to avoid the discomfort of a real ending tends not to help. When the friendship mainly serves to keep a foot in the door or to dodge grief, the research suggests it is more likely to stall moving forward than to support it, even when it is framed as maturity.

Assuming there is one correct rule — that everyone should cut contact, or that everyone should stay friends — does not fit the evidence. Outcomes vary with motives, feelings, and how things ended, so a blanket policy in either direction can be the wrong call for a given situation.

Maintaining a close friendship while one person quietly hopes to rekindle the relationship is the pattern most consistently linked with poorer outcomes, including jealousy and prolonged difficulty letting go. Pretending the feelings are not there rarely makes the friendship the healthy kind.
realNumbersInContext: This is a question where motives matter more than headline percentages, and much of the relevant research is based on surveys and self-report rather than large national datasets — so it is best read as describing patterns and tendencies, not fixed odds. The recurring finding is that friendship- and practicality-based reasons are associated with better outcomes than reasons rooted in unresolved romantic or sexual hope.

Because attachment style and the nature of the breakup also shape how continued contact goes, two people in seemingly similar situations can have very different experiences. Treat the research as a map of what tends to help or hinder, rather than as a prediction of how any individual friendship with an ex will turn out.

faqs.question: Is it healthy to stay friends with an ex?
faqs.answer: It can be, and it can also stall healing — it depends on the reasons and feelings involved. Research suggests friendships grounded in genuine liking or practical ties, where both people have moved on, tend to fare better, while those rooted in unresolved romantic hope tend to fare worse.

faqs.question: Why do some people stay friends with exes and others don't?
faqs.answer: Research by Mogilski and Welling found people stay in touch for varied motives — genuine friendship, practicality like shared kids or finances, sentimentality, or lingering romantic or sexual hope. Those different reasons are associated with different outcomes, which helps explain why experiences vary so much.

faqs.question: Does staying friends stop you from moving on?
faqs.answer: It can, particularly when the friendship serves to avoid the discomfort of a real ending or when one person still hopes to rekindle things. The research on post-breakup adjustment broadly supports giving strong feelings time to settle before attempting a close friendship.

faqs.question: Does it matter how the relationship ended?
faqs.answer: Yes. Research suggests mutual or amicable breakups, and people who are more securely attached, tend to navigate post-relationship friendship more smoothly, while a contested ending or anxious attachment can make continued contact harder and slower to settle.

faqs.question: What if we share children or finances?
faqs.answer: Ongoing practical ties are a common and reasonable basis for staying in contact. A workable, lower-intimacy relationship focused on those shared responsibilities is distinct from a close friendship, which the research finds more contingent on both people having moved on emotionally.
